comments.text:
The halting problem says there's no foolproof way for a computer to check if a program will ever stop. But I think advanced AI systems that split up tasks among specialized subsystems can achieve human-like smarts without solving the halting problem directly. 

It's like a basketball team working together to win, even if no single player can do it all. So while the halting problem is an interesting concept, it likely won't keep AI from progressing, especially if we design AI to coordinate different sub-programs intelligently. That approach basically bypasses the halting problem.

AGI is looking more and more plausible with agentic flows that will allow models to "check their train of thought" before output.

comments.author: @2hcy
comments.text:
Starting training "GPT-5" whatever that really refers to doesn't make sense yet. Let's define GPT-5 as the next generation LLMs. Here's why they haven't started (or just started in the last few weeks): we know that GPT-4 was trained on a large fraction of available high quality text (and some fraction of images). We also know from Chinchila that scaling laws require for a fixed amount of compute, an optimal amount of data. The data size (specifically text data) required to train GPT-5 is an order of magnitude larger than the text available in 2022 and before. You really need to generate synthetic data to scale further. The exact amount is not public information but from my calculations, to generate 10x the internet of text using GPT-4, you need about $10B in inference costs alone. GPT-4 cost $50-100M to train. Going from $100M spend to a $10B in a single go is a tough sell. It will happen eventually, and yes, it's possible the data quality of synth data is much higher so maybe you only need 4x the internet worth of text but it still really takes a ton of compute and time to build that dataset. There's also a ton of research and experiments that has to go into optimizing the processes of creating such a massive dataset and ensuring it has the diversity needed to really push into the next generation. I think OpenAI is playing the long game as is Meta with not releasing a llama 3 yet. There are also a ton of challenges with aligning and red teaming these larger agentic systems so you can bet that once GPT-5 is trained, it will be at least 8 months before anyone outside OpenAI and Microsoft Research get to play with it. 

One fun fact I'll throw in: notice how the company that is best at AI safety and alignment research, namely Anthropic, also has the #1 LLM today (Opus)? That's not a coincidence. It's because the interpretability methods that allow for AI systems to be aligned also provide insights on how to improve the models to be more capable.

Should be able to solve a halting problem with a monitor. That looks at the initial prompt and compares the current output and process to reach the output and is satisfied if the most recent output meets the initial prompt.

Testing for this can be done using games that have points where winning for the opponent is basically impossible from there forward but the game has not closed. Zugzwang chess, Go's equivalent, 2:1 unit over power in RTS, when DOTs or game mechanics(like cutscenes will interrupt and "win" the encounter). You would train the monitor to find these sorts of events, and then "decide" when to interrupt the play of the other model. Once the monitor can predict win scenarios in the games that sort of "is a win at hand" can then just be an alert to the human prompter to bring them back to the play AI to see how satisfactory the result is. I would focus on more complicated games given the direction that the agents seems to be trending, MMOs being a prime candidate, as each individual role would have zero understanding of "win" only how to tank/heal/damage. comments.author: @Jacksplague
comments.text: The seamless fusion of these two models (RL+transformer) is what I would consider AGI. In my opinion the transformer model is advancing faster because we are developing it for the correct environment (reasoning). Reinforcement learning is better suited towards "brute force" problems, where the only way that the model can perform adequately is for it to compile data from direct input streams. I like to think of it in a biological sense.... A baby sticks puts random things in it's mouth to determine it's use/properties (including their own foot to define what is them, and what isn't). The "RL" portion of their brain catalogs this stream of data for later use by the reasoning portion. There is some overlap, but neither of these models can do the other's "job" as well. When they are able to seamlessly share between each other to tackle problems, or divide and conquer different aspects of a problem simultaneously we will begin to see just how powerful AI can be.

comments.author: @GrumpDog
comments.text: The "halting problem" is not a real problem that will have any impact on AI progress. It's just a pointless thought-experiment, a paradox within abstract reasoning, not something that actually prevents us from achieving anything real. It is nothing more than an example of a theoretical decision problem which is inherently undecidable. Clearly it does not prevent humans from doing what they do, so it will not prevent us from recreating what humans do, within machines.

comments.author: @NanoAGI
comments.text: Just so you know, All AI, Robotics, computer science, etc.. started out of DARPA. DARPA has been around a long time, and funds projects at Universities and small, med business. There are call for proposals many times a year, you can see them online. All of the Neural Network, self driving cars, planning architectures and most of the earlier papers were all funded under grants from DARPA or other various Government research organizations. It's easy to think that all these big corporations are the First to come up with this, but it's not true. I think LLM's are great, but its not going to give you AGI without other non LLM systems connected. LLM's are obviously an early technology and it's unclear how far they will be able to go, and there seems to be much hype by companies trying to get money or position themselves as the end all. Just take stuff with a grain of salt. But these are exciting times and more people are interested in AI then ever before, which is a good thing and will drive innovations.
